k8s-004.approach: Split the read into who asks, which server and namespace, which API group and resource, which object name and which verb.
k8s-004.why: Authorization in this lesson is evaluated per request tuple, so `get` on `deployments.apps/hello` in the leased namespace is a different question from the same verb in another namespace.
k8s-004.pitfall: Writing only `hello` and `get` omits the caller and namespace, so the record could describe a read against an ambient context the lease never authorized.
k8s-004.verify: The tuple must translate field by field into one `kubectl auth can-i get deployments.apps/hello` command with explicit kubeconfig, context and namespace flags.

k8s-004.approach: Match each of the three requests against the Role rules, requiring verb, resource and resourceNames to agree within a single rule.
k8s-004.why: The example Role names `hello` under `resourceNames` with only `get`, so a list of all Deployments has no matching rule, and Namespaces are cluster-scoped and cannot be granted by a namespaced Role at all.
k8s-004.pitfall: Assuming `get` on one Deployment implies `list` treats verbs as a hierarchy, but RBAC verbs are independent strings and list returns every object, including ones the name restriction excludes.
k8s-004.verify: Exactly one of the three requests (get hello) should have a fully matching rule; the other two should have none.

k8s-004.approach: Compare `metadata.uid` from the ns-1 receipt with the uid in the ns-2 readback before looking at any other field.
k8s-004.why: A namespace UID is assigned by the API server at creation, so a deleted and recreated namespace keeps its name and labels but receives a new UID.
k8s-004.pitfall: Accepting the readback because the name and owner label both match would let a stale receipt act on a replacement namespace that another process may now own.
k8s-004.verify: The two UIDs differ, so the decision is refuse; changing the label or name in your notes must not flip that answer.

k8s-004.approach: Ask the server about one permitted own-namespace action and one action the identity should lack, such as listing Secrets or reading Nodes, under the explicit lease.
k8s-004.why: Only the server's answer for this identity at this time reflects every binding that applies, which the single Role file cannot show.
k8s-004.pitfall: Recording the Role YAML as the result skips the observation, and pasting the kubeconfig to prove the identity would leak the credential the exercise is meant to protect.
k8s-004.verify: Each row names verb, resource and namespace with the server's yes or no, and a text search of the record finds no token or certificate data.

k8s-004.approach: Resolve the binding's scope first (namespace lesson-a), then check each requested resource against the rules of the `view` ClusterRole.
k8s-004.why: A RoleBinding confines whatever role it references to its own namespace, and the built-in `view` role lists Pods but omits Secrets.
k8s-004.pitfall: Reading `ClusterRole` in the roleRef as cluster-wide access would wrongly allow Pods in lesson-b; that scope only comes from a ClusterRoleBinding.
k8s-004.verify: Expect allowed, denied, denied for Pods in lesson-a, Pods in lesson-b and Secrets in lesson-a, matching `kubectl auth can-i` with `--as` and explicit `--namespace`.

k8s-004.approach: Treat the Role as one input to a union of all bindings that reference the identity, its groups and any ServiceAccount it uses.
k8s-004.why: Kubernetes RBAC is purely additive with no deny rules, so another RoleBinding or a ClusterRoleBinding to a group can add permissions this file never mentions.
k8s-004.pitfall: Concluding least privilege from the narrow Role alone ignores group bindings such as a ClusterRoleBinding for `system:authenticated`, which could grant far more.
k8s-004.verify: Name at least one binding outside the file that could widen access and cite `kubectl auth can-i --list` in the leased namespace as the effective set.

k8s-005.approach: Read the container block of the starter field by field: image, imagePullPolicy, command and the first ports entry.
k8s-005.why: These four fields fully determine which preloaded image tag the kubelet may use, that it must not pull, which fixture process starts and which port name later objects can reference.
k8s-005.pitfall: Quoting the lesson title or guessing from the file name skips the YAML, and would miss that `Never` forbids a registry pull rather than merely preferring a cache.
k8s-005.verify: Each answer cites an exact path under `spec.template.spec.containers[0]` and reads 0.2.0, Never, the fixed server command and 8080 named http.

k8s-005.approach: Classify phase and readiness as separate signals, then change only the readinessProbe path from /missing back to /ready.
k8s-005.why: The fixture server keeps running when /missing returns an error, so the phase stays Running while the Ready condition stays False until the probe succeeds.
k8s-005.pitfall: Calling the first Run a crash would send you to the command or image, yet restartCount stays unchanged because a readiness failure never restarts the container.
k8s-005.verify: The first result names the failed readiness check, and the second Run reports the Ready condition True for a new Pod.

k8s-005.approach: Place each failure on the timeline: broker admission before any API object, or kubelet image handling after the Pod is accepted and scheduled.
k8s-005.why: An unapproved image is refused by the broker allowlist, while ErrImageNeverPull appears only when an accepted Pod with pull policy Never lands on a node lacking the image.
k8s-005.pitfall: Rebuilding application code treats both as runtime crashes, but in neither case did the container process start, so code changes cannot help.
k8s-005.verify: State object created no and process started no for the broker case, object created yes and process started no for ErrImageNeverPull.

k8s-005.approach: Attach Pod UID, container name and restartCount to the bounded excerpt before interpreting the line.
k8s-005.why: Pod names repeat across replacements and `--previous` can return output from an earlier container instance, so only those three fields pin the line to one process.
k8s-005.pitfall: Copying the newest lines by Pod name could mix output from a replaced Pod with the same generated name pattern, or a previous container after a restart.
k8s-005.verify: A second reader finds the same UID, container name and restartCount in a readback; the excerpt contains no secrets or unrelated workloads.

k8s-005.approach: Compare metadata.uid first and only then interpret restartCount within one Pod.
k8s-005.why: restartCount counts kubelet restarts of a container inside one Pod object, while a new UID means a controller created a different Pod with a fresh count of 0.
k8s-005.pitfall: Reading the drop from 1 to 0 as a counter reset inside one Pod hides the replacement and the loss of that Pod's emptyDir data.
k8s-005.verify: Same UID with count 1 is a container restart; different UID with count 0 is a new Pod instance.

k8s-005.approach: List what this source creates (a Deployment and its Pods only) and map each claim to a named check in the Run result.
k8s-005.why: The Deployment-only starter has no Service, so the run can observe controller ownership, Ready Pod identities and cleanup but no Service routing or client response.
k8s-005.pitfall: Borrowing a Service success line from k8s-008 would claim traffic evidence for an object that this manifest never creates.
k8s-005.verify: Every sentence in your statement points to a check name, and any Service or client claim without one is deleted.

k8s-006.approach: Walk ownerReferences upward from each Pod to its ReplicaSet and from that ReplicaSet to the Deployment, recording UIDs at each hop.
k8s-006.why: The `controller: true` reference is set by the ReplicaSet controller itself, so a UID chain proves ownership in a way a shared app label cannot.
k8s-006.pitfall: Drawing the graph from `app=hello` labels would include any unrelated Pod carrying that label and overstate the replica set.
k8s-006.verify: Exactly two Pods link through one ReplicaSet UID to the intended Deployment UID, and every arrow cites the UID it follows.

k8s-006.approach: Compare metadata.generation 4 with status.observedGeneration 3 before reading readyReplicas.
k8s-006.why: The API server bumps generation on every spec change, and the Deployment controller copies it to observedGeneration only after processing, so 3 means spec 4 is unprocessed.
k8s-006.pitfall: Accepting readyReplicas 2 as success reports the health of the generation 3 template, which may differ from the spec you just applied.
k8s-006.verify: The conclusion cites observedGeneration below generation and states the latest desired state is not yet observed.

k8s-006.approach: Edit only spec.replicas from 1 to 2, then Run and read the result as a new baseline rather than a change to an old one.
k8s-006.why: The ReplicaSet controller creates one additional Pod to meet the count of 2, and the browser operation records its own Run identity and cleanup.
k8s-006.pitfall: Reusing the fixture's illustrative Pod names as evidence would make the result look valid without any server-assigned UID behind it.
k8s-006.verify: The result lists two distinct Ready Pod UIDs and a cleanup entry carrying this Run's identity.

k8s-006.approach: Delete exactly one recorded Pod by UID precondition, then wait a bounded time for the ReplicaSet to restore the count.
k8s-006.why: The ReplicaSet still wants two replicas, so it creates a new Pod from the unchanged template while the Deployment generation stays the same.
k8s-006.pitfall: Deleting by label selector could remove both Pods or an unrelated one, and rolling the Deployment would wrongly create a new ReplicaSet revision.
k8s-006.verify: The packet shows the Deployment UID and generation unchanged, one Pod UID removed and one new UID added.

k8s-006.approach: Filter the list to Pods whose controller ownerReference resolves to the intended ReplicaSet UID, then count Ready ones.
k8s-006.why: The foreign Pod belongs to a different controller, so it cannot satisfy this ReplicaSet's replica contract even though its labels and phase match.
k8s-006.pitfall: Counting `app=hello` Pods in phase Running returns 2 and passes a broken Deployment that actually has only one owned replica.
k8s-006.verify: Owned Ready count is 1 against a raw list length of 2, so acceptance fails.

k8s-006.approach: Separate the final status snapshot from a time series of client requests sampled during the replacement window.
k8s-006.why: The Deployment status reports only the end state, while capacity was reduced between deletion and the new Pod becoming Ready.
k8s-006.pitfall: Citing readyReplicas 2 afterward as proof that no request failed assumes continuity the status field never measured.
k8s-006.verify: Name the client timeline with timestamps, outcomes and error counts as the measurement no Deployment status field can provide.

k8s-007.approach: Compare each key and value in the Service spec.selector with the labels in the Deployment Pod template, treating the selector as a set query.
k8s-007.why: A Service selects every Pod in its namespace whose labels contain all selector pairs, so app=hello matches the template label and app=wrong matches nothing in this manifest.
k8s-007.pitfall: Checking only that a Service named hello exists misses the selector entirely; the object is accepted with app=wrong and simply has zero endpoints.
k8s-007.verify: Key and value agree exactly for app=hello; for app=wrong the value differs, so the intended set is empty.

k8s-007.approach: Follow the chain from the Service port to targetPort, then resolve the name `http` against the container ports list.
k8s-007.why: A string targetPort is looked up by name on each selected container, and this container declares `http` once as containerPort 8080.
k8s-007.pitfall: Assuming targetPort must equal port numerically would break as soon as the Service port changes, and a misspelled port name still creates a valid Service that routes nowhere.
k8s-007.verify: The chain reads 8080 to `http` to 8080, and `http` appears exactly once in the container ports list.

k8s-007.approach: Collect every targetRef.uid from the four EndpointSlice entries and reduce them to a set before comparing with the owned Ready Pods.
k8s-007.why: The same Pod can appear in more than one slice or once per IP family, so only distinct UIDs measure distinct backends.
k8s-007.pitfall: Counting endpoint rows reports four backends and would also hide a foreign UID among them.
k8s-007.verify: The set holds exactly two UIDs, and it equals the owned Ready Pod UIDs recorded independently.

k8s-007.approach: Run the starter with selector app=wrong unchanged, keep its failure record, then restore app=hello and submit a separate Run.
k8s-007.why: No Pod carries app=wrong, so the Service never gains a ready endpoint and the bounded backend check fails before the client step.
k8s-007.pitfall: Editing the selector and rerunning without first recording the failure loses the negative evidence, and treating the second Run as a patch of the first ignores that each Run creates and deletes its own Service.
k8s-007.verify: The record shows the exact app=wrong selector, the failed check name and cleanup, then a separate passing Run with new UIDs.

k8s-007.approach: Check that the client Job's UID belongs to this Run, then compare its output with the `/version` payload contract.
k8s-007.why: The client Pod resolves the Service name and receives the fixture response only if selector, port chain and readiness all line up.
k8s-007.pitfall: Accepting Job completion alone would pass a client that called `/ready`, which proves probe health, not the version payload.
k8s-007.verify: Job and Pod ownership match this Run, exit status is 0 and the output equals ds60-fixture-v1.

k8s-007.approach: Specify a new Service name with its own receipt and repeat the selector, port, backend and client checks against that object only.
k8s-007.why: A distinct owned receipt and UID-aware cleanup keep the experiment from mutating the shared `hello` Service or another learner's objects.
k8s-007.pitfall: Editing the hello Service selector in place to test the idea would change the baseline other checks depend on and cannot be undone by UID.
k8s-007.verify: The design names its own Service, its own receipt and a UID-scoped delete, and never edits hello.

k8s-009.approach: Trace hello-config and key message into both consumers: the configMapKeyRef env entry and the lesson-config volume mounted at /config.
k8s-009.why: The env entry and the volume both name the same ConfigMap and key, while the volume name links the Pod volume to a read-only container mount.
k8s-009.pitfall: Matching only the ConfigMap name would miss a wrong key, which leaves the env var unresolved and blocks container start even though the object exists.
k8s-009.verify: Every reference resolves inside the manifest and the projected file path is /config/message with readOnly true.

k8s-009.approach: Add the ConfigMap, the DS60_MESSAGE reference and the read-only volume, then Run under a fresh contract-2 lease.
k8s-009.why: The fixed client calls `/message` for the environment path and `/file-message` for the mounted path, so both consumers must return reviewer.
k8s-009.pitfall: Treating a Ready Pod as success ignores that readiness only checks `/ready` and says nothing about which configuration either path loaded.
k8s-009.verify: The result shows three passing checks for `/version`, `/message` and `/file-message` plus cleanup of the ConfigMap, Deployment and Service.

k8s-009.approach: Hold the process fixed and ask what reads the environment and when.
k8s-009.why: The kubelet resolves configMapKeyRef once when the container starts, so the running process keeps hello after the ConfigMap changes.
k8s-009.pitfall: Expecting `/message` to switch to reviewer after an edit assumes live environment updates, which Kubernetes never performs for a running process.
k8s-009.verify: Pod UID and restartCount are unchanged, and the environment value stays hello until a new process starts.

k8s-009.approach: Record three observations with timestamps: the ConfigMap value from the API, the bytes in /config/message and the application's HTTP answer.
k8s-009.why: Volume projections are refreshed by the kubelet on its own sync cycle, and the fixture rereads the file per request, so each stage can lag the previous one.
k8s-009.pitfall: Assuming the file updates immediately or on a fixed delay would turn a guess into a transcript; any timing claim must come from an owned observation.
k8s-009.verify: Each record cites its source and time, and absent the host capability the record stays labeled synthetic.

k8s-009.approach: Add one unsupported field at a time in a scratch copy and Run each, then restore the approved source.
k8s-009.why: The broker allowlist refuses secretKeyRef, hostPath, subPath and arbitrary env before any API request, so no object is created.
k8s-009.pitfall: Describing a refusal as a ConfigMap error blames the cluster for a rejection the course adapter produced before submission.
k8s-009.verify: Each refusal message is recorded with no create receipt, and the restored source still passes the parse step.

k8s-009.approach: Write before and after rows with ConfigMap UID and resourceVersion, Pod UIDs and the routes observed, plus the source to restore.
k8s-009.why: Because env values bind at start, a release needs new Pods, and rollback needs the exact prior ConfigMap content and fresh Pods consuming it.
k8s-009.pitfall: Deleting objects by name to roll back cannot tell an old Pod from a replacement and leaves no evidence that the old message is served again.
k8s-009.verify: A reviewer can roll back using only the recorded UIDs, resourceVersion and restored source, then confirm `/message` returns the old value.

k8s-010.approach: Read requests and limits as two mappings, note they start equal at 100m and 64Mi, then edit only the requests to 10m and 16Mi.
k8s-010.why: The scheduler and ResourceQuota sum requests, while the kubelet and runtime enforce limits, so lowering requests changes placement but keeps the same ceiling.
k8s-010.pitfall: Lowering limits instead would tighten the runtime ceiling and risk an OOM kill at 16Mi without changing anything the scheduler sees.
k8s-010.verify: The edited source shows requests 10m/16Mi and limits 100m/64Mi, and the scheduler is named as the requests reader.

k8s-010.approach: Multiply each request by spec.replicas, then expand 64Mi with powers of two.
k8s-010.why: Two replicas at 10m and 16Mi request 20m and 32Mi, and 64 times 1,048,576 is 67,108,864 bytes.
k8s-010.pitfall: Using decimal megabytes gives 64,000,000 bytes, which disagrees with the Mi suffix and with the offline check.
k8s-010.verify: The numbers match the assertions in the offline check script exactly.

k8s-010.approach: Set request 200m and limit 100m in a scratch source and submit it.
k8s-010.why: A request above its limit is invalid, and the course broker refuses it before any API call, so no Pod is created or scheduled.
k8s-010.pitfall: Reading the refusal as a scheduling failure assumes the Pod reached the scheduler, but no object exists to schedule.
k8s-010.verify: The result shows the refusal text and no created resource UID.

k8s-010.approach: Ask first whether the Pod object was admitted, then whether spec.nodeName was set.
k8s-010.why: A Forbidden exceeded quota error comes from admission before the Pod exists, while Pending with FailedScheduling means the Pod exists but no node fits its requests.
k8s-010.pitfall: Reading container logs for either record finds nothing, because in neither case did a container start.
k8s-010.verify: Quota maps to admission with no object; FailedScheduling maps to an admitted Pod with empty nodeName.

k8s-010.approach: Look for reason OOMKilled in state.terminated or lastState.terminated before interpreting exit code 137.
k8s-010.why: OOMKilled is set when the container exceeded its memory limit, whereas 137 only says the process received SIGKILL, which several causes produce.
k8s-010.pitfall: Calling every 137 an OOM kill and raising the memory limit could hide a liveness kill or an external termination.
k8s-010.verify: Only the record carrying reason OOMKilled is classified as memory enforcement; the bare 137 stays unconfirmed.

k8s-010.approach: Choose one failure record, change exactly one field that addresses its mechanism and state acceptance in terms of the failed stage.
k8s-010.why: A quota failure clears when requests fit the quota, a scheduling failure when a node can fit the request, and an OOM kill when usage stays under the limit.
k8s-010.pitfall: Raising every request and limit at once may make the Pod Ready but cannot show which change fixed it and may exceed the namespace budget.
k8s-010.verify: The diff touches one field and acceptance names admission, placement or termination reason as the observed recovery.

k8s-011.approach: Read completions and parallelism from spec, restartPolicy from the Pod template, then backoffLimit and activeDeadlineSeconds, and edit the last two.
k8s-011.why: The starter needs one success, runs one Pod at a time, never restarts in place, allows one retry and stops at 30 seconds; the edit sets backoffLimit 0 and 20 seconds.
k8s-011.pitfall: Setting restartPolicy to OnFailure to remove retries moves restarts into the Pod rather than removing them.
k8s-011.verify: Quoted values read 1, 1, Never, 0 and 20 seconds from your edited YAML.

k8s-011.approach: Run the success outcome and compare the output ledger against the expected values field by field.
k8s-011.why: The fixed task is deterministic, so a correct run prints accepted 3, rejected 2 and total 35 and exits 0.
k8s-011.pitfall: Trusting the Complete condition without reading the ledger could accept a task that exited 0 with wrong totals.
k8s-011.verify: Ledger fields match exactly and the task Pod's controller ownerReference is this Run's Job UID.

k8s-011.approach: Change only the outcome value to failure and Run it.
k8s-011.why: The manifest is still valid and the container starts, so the Job controller records a nonzero exit and marks the Job Failed when backoff is exhausted.
k8s-011.pitfall: Treating Failed as a manifest problem sends you to the YAML, yet the API accepted it and the container ran.
k8s-011.verify: The Job condition is Failed, the container exit code is nonzero and cleanup names the same Job UID.

k8s-011.approach: Count new Pods per backoffLimit value, keeping restartPolicy Never in mind.
k8s-011.why: With Never, each failed attempt is a separate Pod, so backoffLimit 0 allows one Pod and backoffLimit 1 allows up to two.
k8s-011.pitfall: Reading Never as no retries at all confuses kubelet restarts within a Pod with Job controller retries across Pods.
k8s-011.verify: Expect at most one task Pod at backoffLimit 0 and at most two at backoffLimit 1, with restartCount staying 0 in each.

k8s-011.approach: Read schedule, timeZone, suspend, concurrencyPolicy and startingDeadlineSeconds from the fixture and state each effect.
k8s-011.why: The five-minute schedule in UTC is defined, but suspend true stops new Jobs from being created, and existing Jobs keep running.
k8s-011.pitfall: Assuming suspend deletes active Jobs or proves past runs would mistake a future scheduling switch for cleanup or history.
k8s-011.verify: Each field is named with its effect and the conclusion says no new Job starts while suspended.

k8s-011.approach: Give each logical unit of work a stable key and publish its effect through a check that rejects a key already committed.
k8s-011.why: The Job controller may start a second Pod after an attempt that already wrote its effect, so the sink must dedupe on the key.
k8s-011.pitfall: Relying on backoffLimit 0 to prevent duplicates fails because a node loss or deadline can still yield a second Pod.
k8s-011.verify: Simulate a crash after the write and before the acknowledgment; the retry finds the key and publishes nothing new.

k8s-012.approach: Lay out the five boundaries as a dependency chain and, for each case, stop at the first boundary with no supporting evidence.
k8s-012.why: Each stage needs the previous one: a container cannot start before the Pod is scheduled, and a client response needs a Ready endpoint first.
k8s-012.pitfall: Opening application logs first for every case fails for case A, where the container was never created and there are no logs to read.
k8s-012.verify: Each case has one first failed boundary and every later boundary is marked not reached.

k8s-012.approach: Read the configMapKeyRef in the Pod spec and check that the named ConfigMap and key exist in the same namespace.
k8s-012.why: A missing ConfigMap or key stops the kubelet at container configuration with CreateContainerConfigError, before any process runs.
k8s-012.pitfall: Calling case A a crash and raising restart tolerance changes nothing, because restartCount stays 0 and no process ever exited.
k8s-012.verify: The check quotes the ConfigMap name and key exactly as the spec does and needs no application log.

k8s-012.approach: Change only readinessProbe.httpGet.path from /missing to /ready and predict the two confirming observations.
k8s-012.why: The fixture serves 200 on /ready and 404 on /missing, so the process runs normally but stays unready until the probe path is fixed.
k8s-012.pitfall: Editing the Service selector or resource limits leaves the 404 untouched, so the Pod remains NotReady and the client still gets no endpoint.
k8s-012.verify: A new Run shows the Ready condition True and a successful client response, with one field changed.

k8s-012.approach: Read the Job's terminal condition together with the task container's terminated exit code.
k8s-012.why: Exit code 2 from a started container with condition Failed means the task itself reported failure, not the controller or the image.
k8s-012.pitfall: Raising backoffLimit retries the same deterministic input, so every attempt exits 2 and the Job still fails, only later.
k8s-012.verify: The record cites Failed and exit 2 together, and shows neither DeadlineExceeded nor an image waiting reason.

k8s-012.approach: Write four rows for one case: what you observed, what you inferred, the one change you made and the condition that would accept it.
k8s-012.why: Separating observation from hypothesis lets a reviewer see which field or log line supported each step and which belief was later disproved.
k8s-012.pitfall: Rewriting the timeline after the fix to show only the successful step erases the failed hypothesis that ruled out a cause.
k8s-012.verify: Every row cites an object UID and a bounded field or line, and synthetic rows are labeled.

k8s-012.approach: List the check that failed originally plus the end-to-end client result, then the UIDs you created and nothing else.
k8s-012.why: Recovery is proven at the layer that broke, and cleanup is safe only against identities you recorded at creation.
k8s-012.pitfall: Deleting every object labeled app=hello would remove same-name replacements or another learner's objects the run never created.
k8s-012.verify: Post-repair checks pass, and the delete list matches the creation record UID for UID.

k8s-013.approach: Diff revision A against B and classify each changed path as inside or outside spec.template.
k8s-013.why: The Deployment controller hashes only the Pod template, so a changed template annotation creates a new ReplicaSet while the Deployment name and UID stay the same.
k8s-013.pitfall: Treating a changed spec.replicas or a Deployment-level annotation as a new revision would expect a ReplicaSet that never appears.
k8s-013.verify: Every change in the B example falls under spec.template, so one new pod-template-hash is expected.

k8s-013.approach: Group Pods by ownerReference to their ReplicaSet and count Ready Pods per pod-template-hash.
k8s-013.why: At generation 5 the old ReplicaSet still holds Ready Pods that serve traffic while the candidate's Pods fail readiness.
k8s-013.pitfall: Accepting the aggregate readyReplicas count would call the rollout healthy while every Ready Pod still runs revision A.
k8s-013.verify: The candidate hash has zero or too few Ready Pods, so B is incomplete.

k8s-013.approach: Write the gate as named conditions with a single deadline: observedGeneration, updatedReplicas, candidate ready count and the application marker.
k8s-013.why: Together these show the controller processed the spec, the new template is fully replaced and the served response belongs to B.
k8s-013.pitfall: Waiting with no deadline lets a stalled rollout block the lease, and accepting on Available alone ignores which version is available.
k8s-013.verify: Each condition maps to one readback or request and reports its own failure when the deadline passes.

k8s-013.approach: Pick revert or fix explicitly, apply it as a new change and reobserve generation and marker.
k8s-013.why: Both choices bump metadata.generation, so success needs observedGeneration to catch up and the served marker to match the chosen source.
k8s-013.pitfall: Reporting the rollout undo command as the outcome describes the request, not whether the controller converged.
k8s-013.verify: observedGeneration equals the new generation and the response marker matches the restored or fixed source.

k8s-013.approach: List both image digests, the manifests that reference them and a response that differs between the two binaries.
k8s-013.why: Only digests pin exact artifacts, and a version endpoint that returns different values per binary proves which one served the request.
k8s-013.pitfall: Changing a message in one image and calling it a version roll proves configuration, not a binary change.
k8s-013.verify: The plan names two digests and a response check that distinguishes them.

k8s-013.approach: Describe periodic client requests during the rollout with interval, per-request version and error tallies.
k8s-013.why: Only sampled requests show which revision answered and whether any failed while old and new Pods coexisted.
k8s-013.pitfall: Quoting the final rollout status as zero downtime claims continuity no snapshot recorded.
k8s-013.verify: The answer names interval, per-sample result and error count, and makes no universal uptime claim.

k8s-014.approach: Add the ConfigMap and its two consumers to the k8s-008 source, then trace every reference with the field that creates it.
k8s-014.why: Selector, configMapKeyRef and volume name are lookups by name or label, while ownership only appears later from the controllers.
k8s-014.pitfall: Drawing ownerReferences between source objects invents links the YAML cannot contain, because they are written by controllers at runtime.
k8s-014.verify: Each arrow carries selector, configMapKeyRef or volume name, and two replicas with matching app labels are identified.

k8s-014.approach: Follow the Run result's ownership chain from Deployment to current ReplicaSet to each Ready Pod.
k8s-014.why: Only Pods controlled by the current ReplicaSet count toward this generation's desired replicas.
k8s-014.pitfall: Counting all Pods with app=hello could include an old ReplicaSet's Pod or an unrelated one and still show two.
k8s-014.verify: Exactly two owned Ready Pod UIDs sit under the current ReplicaSet.

k8s-014.approach: Compare the endpoint UID set with the owned Ready set, then each response with the fixed version and both message values.
k8s-014.why: Matching sets show the Service routes only to this Deployment's Pods, and exact values show the configuration reached both the environment and volume consumers.
k8s-014.pitfall: Checking only the version value would pass even if the ConfigMap key were wrong, since version does not depend on the message.
k8s-014.verify: UID sets are equal and the version and both message values match the contract exactly.

k8s-014.approach: Pick one admitted fault, such as selector app=wrong, write which check will fail, then Run.
k8s-014.why: Each fault breaks one link: a wrong selector empties endpoints, a wrong probe path keeps Pods unready and a failing task fails its Job.
k8s-014.pitfall: Running several faults at once makes it impossible to say which change caused the failed check.
k8s-014.verify: The failed check matches your written prediction and cleanup lists only this Run's UIDs.

k8s-014.approach: Restore the faulted field and submit a new Run, then compare checks and identities with the failed one.
k8s-014.why: The browser cleans up after every Run, so the repaired Run creates fresh objects and is a new observation.
k8s-014.pitfall: Describing the repair as patching the earlier Service assumes state that was already deleted.
k8s-014.verify: Every UID differs between Runs and the previously failing check now passes.

k8s-014.approach: Assemble source, target identity without secrets and evidence for each claim, and list the surfaces not qualified.
k8s-014.why: A second learner can reproduce the reasoning only when each claim points to evidence in the packet itself.
k8s-014.pitfall: Writing production ready or always available adds claims no bounded Run measured.
k8s-014.verify: A second learner finds evidence for every claim using the packet alone.

k8s-015.approach: For each probe, name the component that acts on failure and the action it takes.
k8s-015.why: Startup failure past its threshold kills the container, readiness failure removes the Pod from endpoints and liveness failure restarts the container.
k8s-015.pitfall: Treating all three as one health flag would predict a restart for a readiness failure, which never restarts anything.
k8s-015.verify: Three different actions are listed: gate later probes, withhold traffic, restart.

k8s-015.approach: Add the delay variable and both probes, compute the startup budget, then Run.
k8s-015.why: The startupProbe allows 1 times 10 equals 10 seconds, more than the 3-second delay, and liveness only begins after startup succeeds.
k8s-015.pitfall: Putting failureThreshold 2 on the startupProbe would give 2 seconds, so the kubelet would kill the container before /startup ever succeeds.
k8s-015.verify: Configured budget 10 seconds exceeds delay 3, and observed times are reported separately.

k8s-015.approach: Classify case A as a readiness failure and list the recovery evidence it would need.
k8s-015.why: Readiness failure only removes the Pod from EndpointSlices; the container keeps running with the same restartCount.
k8s-015.pitfall: Expecting a restart and waiting for restartCount to change watches the wrong field.
k8s-015.verify: The answer cites a Ready condition change and an endpoint or client observation, not a restart.

k8s-015.approach: Compare Pod UID and restartCount between the two case B records.
k8s-015.why: A liveness failure makes the kubelet restart the container inside the same Pod, so UID stays and restartCount increases.
k8s-015.pitfall: Calling it a replacement would expect a new UID and a reset count, neither of which appears.
k8s-015.verify: UID is identical and restartCount went up by at least one.

k8s-015.approach: Change one probe path to /missing in a scratch copy, Run it and record what the bounded result actually shows.
k8s-015.why: /missing returns 404, so a startup or liveness probe on it fails, but how many restarts or how long depends on timing you must observe.
k8s-015.pitfall: Writing a fixed failure time from periodSeconds alone invents a measurement the result never contained.
k8s-015.verify: The record holds the actual Run outcome and cleanup and no unobserved timing.

k8s-015.approach: Reserve liveness for states a restart fixes, such as a deadlock, and route dependency outages to readiness or degraded responses.
k8s-015.why: Restarting every caller during a database outage adds cold starts without restoring the dependency.
k8s-015.pitfall: Making liveness call the downstream dependency would restart every replica at once during that outage.
k8s-015.verify: The policy restarts only for repairable local failures and changes readiness or behavior for dependency loss.

k8s-016.approach: Read the Pod spec's initContainers list, then containers, and mark prepare as a gate in front of read.
k8s-016.why: The kubelet runs init containers to completion one at a time and starts application containers only after every init container exits 0.
k8s-016.pitfall: Expecting prepare and read to start together, like two entries in containers, predicts that read may find no file yet.
k8s-016.verify: initContainerStatuses shows prepare terminated with exit 0 before read appears running in containerStatuses.

k8s-016.approach: Follow the name work from spec.volumes to the volumeMounts of both prepare and read.
k8s-016.why: An emptyDir is created once per Pod, so every mount that references the same volume name sees the same directory at /work.
k8s-016.pitfall: Assuming each container gets its own copy because its filesystem is separate would predict read finds nothing the init container wrote.
k8s-016.verify: One emptyDir named work exists, and both mounts reference that name with mountPath /work.

k8s-016.approach: Run the teacher fixture once and compare Pod UID, marker and restartCount across both application attempts.
k8s-016.why: A container restart happens inside the same Pod, so the emptyDir and the marker written by prepare survive while restartCount increments.
k8s-016.pitfall: Expecting prepare to rerun and write a new marker treats a container restart as a Pod restart.
k8s-016.verify: Pod UID and marker match across attempts, and only restartCount changed.

k8s-016.approach: Delete only the recorded owned Pod through the host capability and read the replacement.
k8s-016.why: A new Pod gets a new UID and a new emptyDir, so prepare runs again and writes a fresh marker.
k8s-016.pitfall: Expecting the old marker to persist assumes emptyDir lives outside the Pod, which it does not.
k8s-016.verify: UID and marker both differ, and the old marker is nowhere in the new record.

k8s-016.approach: Start with prepare's state and reason, then name the single mount or permission fix.
k8s-016.why: If an init container fails, the kubelet never starts the application container, so read's absence follows from prepare.
k8s-016.pitfall: Debugging the read container as a second fault chases a container that never started and has no logs.
k8s-016.verify: The init state shows the failure reason, and the proposed repair touches one mount or permission.

k8s-016.approach: Name Pod deletion as the end of the marker and point to a PersistentVolumeClaim and a separate backup as the later contracts.
k8s-016.why: emptyDir is removed when the Pod leaves its node, so nothing written there survives replacement, and no copy exists elsewhere.
k8s-016.pitfall: Calling the shared file persistent because it survived a container restart confuses container lifetime with Pod lifetime.
k8s-016.verify: The answer names Pod deletion and a later storage or backup mechanism that would survive it.

k8s-017.approach: Pair each securityContext field with the specific path it closes.
k8s-017.why: runAsNonRoot blocks UID 0, dropped capabilities remove kernel privileges, allowPrivilegeEscalation false blocks setuid gains, seccomp limits syscalls and readOnlyRootFilesystem blocks image writes.
k8s-017.pitfall: Labeling all five as generic hardening hides that, for example, dropping capabilities does nothing to stop writes to the root filesystem.
k8s-017.verify: Five fields map to five different attack paths.

k8s-017.approach: Run the unchanged nonroot source and keep configured and observed identity in separate rows.
k8s-017.why: The manifest states runAsUser, but only a host readback shows the identity the process actually ran with.
k8s-017.pitfall: Copying runAsUser from the YAML into the observed row reports configuration as if it were runtime evidence.
k8s-017.verify: Accepted source, readiness, cleanup and two identity rows with distinct sources are recorded.

k8s-017.approach: Change one field in a scratch copy and submit it to the course parser.
k8s-017.why: The parser refuses either field locally, and Pod Security marks privileged true as a Baseline violation and allowPrivilegeEscalation true as a Restricted violation.
k8s-017.pitfall: Claiming Baseline would reject allowPrivilegeEscalation true misplaces that control, since only Restricted forbids it.
k8s-017.verify: A refusal message exists, no create receipt exists and the matching Pod Security level is named.

k8s-017.approach: Classify hostPath, hostNetwork and hostPID against the Pod Security Standards controls.
k8s-017.why: All three expose the node: hostPath reaches its filesystem, hostNetwork its network stack and hostPID its process table, so Baseline forbids each.
k8s-017.pitfall: Assuming only Restricted blocks host access would let a baseline namespace admit them, which it does not.
k8s-017.verify: Each variant cites its control and Baseline as the lowest forbidding level.

k8s-017.approach: Read the enforce and enforce-version labels first, then send one allowed and one denied request.
k8s-017.why: Admission depends on the namespace's enforced level and version, so the result is meaningful only alongside those labels.
k8s-017.pitfall: Reporting a denial without the namespace labels cannot show which policy produced it.
k8s-017.verify: Labels, namespace UID and the API server's denial reason are recorded together.

k8s-017.approach: Name what the fixed controls limit and one threat outside them with its control.
k8s-017.why: The securityContext limits what the container process can do on the node, not which API calls or network peers it can reach.
k8s-017.pitfall: Calling the workload secure overall implies coverage of API access and network paths these fields never touch.
k8s-017.verify: The statement names one uncovered threat and the separate control, such as RBAC or a NetworkPolicy.

k8s-018.approach: Write the full ServiceAccount username and keep it apart from token bytes and Role rules.
k8s-018.why: The identity is just a namespaced name; the token proves it and the Role defines what it may do.
k8s-018.pitfall: Pasting the mounted token to show identity leaks a credential without adding anything the name does not already say.
k8s-018.verify: The record reads system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name> and contains no token text.

k8s-018.approach: Read the RoleBinding namespace and the subject namespace as two separate fields.
k8s-018.why: A RoleBinding grants its Role only within its own metadata.namespace, while the subject namespace just identifies which ServiceAccount.
k8s-018.pitfall: Assuming the grant follows the subject's namespace would predict access where the binding does not exist.
k8s-018.verify: The binding namespace is named as the limit on the grant.

k8s-018.approach: For each of the five rows, look for a Role rule matching verb, resource and namespace.
k8s-018.why: RBAC is additive and default deny, so only own-namespace Pod get and list match a rule and everything else is denied.
k8s-018.pitfall: Assuming list on pods implies read on secrets treats resources as a hierarchy RBAC does not have.
k8s-018.verify: Pod reads in the bound namespace are allowed, and every other row is denied for lack of a rule.

k8s-018.approach: Find automountServiceAccountToken false in the Pod source and confirm it in a host readback.
k8s-018.why: With automount disabled, the ServiceAccount admission plugin does not add the projected kube-api-access volume, so no token is mounted.
k8s-018.pitfall: Removing the RoleBinding and calling the workload tokenless still leaves a mounted token that authenticates.
k8s-018.verify: The readback shows automount false and no kube-api-access volume.

k8s-018.approach: Order the steps: guard refuses, release the exact owned session, then prepare a fresh one just before Run.
k8s-018.why: An expired lease must not authorize a request, and a fresh session restores a bounded target without using leftover credentials.
k8s-018.pitfall: Falling back to the default kubeconfig context would send the Run to whatever cluster that context points at.
k8s-018.verify: No step reuses the expired lease or an ambient context.

k8s-018.approach: Record kubectl auth can-i results under the owned receipt with identity, target, verb, resource, result and time.
k8s-018.why: can-i asks the API server's authorizer, so a yes or no is an actual decision for that identity at that time.
k8s-018.pitfall: Inferring results from the Role YAML alone ignores other bindings that might also grant access.
k8s-018.verify: Each row carries its source and time, and no credential text appears.

k8s-019.approach: Base64-decode only the supplied value and re-encode the result to compare.
k8s-019.why: Base64 is a reversible encoding, so a correct decode re-encodes to the exact original bytes.
k8s-019.pitfall: Trimming or adding a trailing newline before encoding changes the bytes and the round trip no longer matches.
k8s-019.verify: Decoded text is DUMMY_LESSON_ONLY and its encoding equals the supplied value byte for byte.

k8s-019.approach: List encoding, RBAC, encryption at rest, TLS transport and application handling with the threat each one addresses.
k8s-019.why: These act at different points: who can read the object, how etcd stores it, how bytes travel and what the process does with them.
k8s-019.pitfall: Treating base64 as protection gives it a threat it never stops, since anyone can decode it.
k8s-019.verify: Five distinct mechanisms appear, and base64 is paired with no threat.

k8s-019.approach: Check direct Secret reads and arbitrary Secret mounts against the worker contract.
k8s-019.why: The normal worker is not granted Secret access, so both attempts fall outside the operation by design.
k8s-019.pitfall: Requesting a broader role to make the test pass would change the contract the exercise is checking.
k8s-019.verify: Both attempts are classified as outside the contract, and no extra permission is requested.

k8s-019.approach: Assign environment, projected file and application output to three separate observations.
k8s-019.why: Environment variables are fixed at container start, while the kubelet can refresh a mounted Secret file, so A and B can coexist.
k8s-019.pitfall: Expecting the environment variable to change to B assumes the kubelet rewrites a running process's environment.
k8s-019.verify: Environment shows A, file is observed separately and output depends on whether the app rereads the file.

k8s-019.approach: Keep identities, access outcomes, reload behavior and synthetic equality checks, and no real values.
k8s-019.why: A reviewer can confirm the mechanism worked from outcomes and synthetic comparisons without seeing any credential.
k8s-019.pitfall: Saving the mounted file to prove the test ran stores secret material in the evidence record.
k8s-019.verify: Every retained field is an identity, an outcome or a synthetic value.

k8s-019.approach: List the synthetic Secret and workload UIDs from the creation record and delete only those.
k8s-019.why: Deleting by recorded UID cannot remove another learner's or a same-name object, and leaves worker permissions untouched.
k8s-019.pitfall: Deleting every Secret in the namespace would remove objects this fixture never created.
k8s-019.verify: Each deleted UID appears in the creation record, and worker permissions are unchanged.

k8s-020.approach: Write the six layers in request order with one observation each.
k8s-020.why: Each layer can fail on its own, so a layer without an observation leaves a gap in the diagnosis.
k8s-020.pitfall: Starting with HTTP alone and calling a timeout a DNS problem skips four layers of evidence.
k8s-020.verify: Each layer names its observation, from resolver answer to HTTP body.

k8s-020.approach: Add the Service with selector app=hello, port 8080 named http and targetPort http, then Run both objects.
k8s-020.why: targetPort http resolves to the container port named http, and the selector picks the Deployment's Pods as endpoints.
k8s-020.pitfall: Setting targetPort to a name the container does not define leaves endpoints with no usable port.
k8s-020.verify: The result shows the owned backend identity check and an exact `/version` body.

k8s-020.approach: Treat NXDOMAIN as a naming fault and check the name, namespace and resolver search path first.
k8s-020.why: NXDOMAIN means the resolver found no record, so the request never reached any Service or Pod.
k8s-020.pitfall: Restarting backends after NXDOMAIN changes nothing the resolver uses.
k8s-020.verify: The next check concerns name, namespace or resolver configuration only.

k8s-020.approach: List missing ready endpoints, wrong port mapping and policy drop as open hypotheses with their discriminating observations.
k8s-020.why: Resolution succeeded, so the fault lies between Service and Pod, and several causes produce the same timeout.
k8s-020.pitfall: Blaming NetworkPolicy without checking EndpointSlices could miss that no Pod was ready.
k8s-020.verify: The answer names the observation, such as empty EndpointSlices, that separates endpoint loss from a policy drop.

k8s-020.approach: Read each response's status and body against the expected route and version.
k8s-020.why: Any HTTP response proves DNS, Service, endpoint and port worked; 404 isolates the path and a wrong version isolates the application.
k8s-020.pitfall: Treating both as network failures ignores that a response arrived at all.
k8s-020.verify: Each case names the layers it proves and the status or body field that differs.

k8s-020.approach: Write the target, allowed client, timeout, expected failing layer and cleanup before running.
k8s-020.why: Naming the failing layer in advance makes the result a test rather than a search, and the timeout keeps it bounded.
k8s-020.pitfall: Running an open cross-namespace probe without a named capability touches objects outside your lease.
k8s-020.verify: The design names capability, target, timeout, expected layer and cleanup.

k8s-021.approach: Read spec.podSelector for the destination and spec.policyTypes for direction, ignoring the from peers.
k8s-021.why: podSelector app=hello chooses which Pods the policy isolates, and policyTypes Ingress means only inbound traffic to them is affected.
k8s-021.pitfall: Reading the client labels under ingress from as the selected Pods would isolate the callers instead of hello.
k8s-021.verify: The answer names app=hello Pods and Ingress only, with no Egress.

k8s-021.approach: List every policy that selects hello and take the union of their allowed sources.
k8s-021.why: NetworkPolicies are additive allow lists; once any policy isolates a Pod, traffic is allowed if any selecting policy permits it.
k8s-021.pitfall: Treating deny-ingress as a rule that overrides allow-client imagines a priority order the API does not define.
k8s-021.verify: The allowed set equals allow-client's sources, and no field orders the policies.

k8s-021.approach: Count the list items under from and read each item's selectors together.
k8s-021.why: Selectors inside one item must all match, while separate items are alternatives, so the indentation of one dash changes AND to OR.
k8s-021.pitfall: Reading two separate items as one combined requirement would predict a deny for traffic that one item alone allows.
k8s-021.verify: One item with two selectors is AND, and two items are OR.

k8s-021.approach: Send both approved client requests before any policy exists and keep caller, payload and target receipt.
k8s-021.why: Without a pre-policy success, a later failure could come from the backend rather than from enforcement.
k8s-021.pitfall: Applying the policy first and testing only afterward leaves no control to compare against.
k8s-021.verify: Both requests succeed with the expected payload before enforcement.

k8s-021.approach: Repeat the same two requests with the same callers and deadline after applying the policies.
k8s-021.why: With only policy state changed, a new failure on the unpermitted path can be attributed to enforcement by the CNI.
k8s-021.pitfall: Testing on a cluster whose CNI does not enforce NetworkPolicy would show both paths succeeding and suggest the policy is wrong.
k8s-021.verify: The permitted path succeeds and the other fails within its deadline.

k8s-021.approach: Record policy and client UIDs and state the protocol and namespace the claim covers.
k8s-021.why: The test only exercised the listed callers and port, so the isolation claim cannot extend to other protocols or hosts.
k8s-021.pitfall: Writing that hello is isolated from everything generalizes from two requests to all traffic.
k8s-021.verify: Cleanup lists only owned UIDs, and the claim states its protocol and namespace.

k8s-022.approach: Follow volumeClaimTemplates name data to the volumeMounts entry and storageClassName to the class.
k8s-022.why: The StatefulSet creates one claim per ordinal from the template, and the mount with the same name places it at /data.
k8s-022.pitfall: Adding a separate PersistentVolumeClaim and referencing it from the Pod template would make all replicas share one claim.
k8s-022.verify: Each link cites a field: template name, mountPath /data and storageClassName.

k8s-022.approach: Run the writer once with exclusive create and record claim UID, PV name and SHA-256.
k8s-022.why: Exclusive create fails if the marker already exists, so a second run cannot silently overwrite the initial data.
k8s-022.pitfall: Writing with plain overwrite would hide an accidental second run behind a new hash.
k8s-022.verify: One receipt holds claim UID, bound PV and marker hash.

k8s-022.approach: Delete only the recorded Pod and compare UID, ordinal name and claim before and after.
k8s-022.why: The StatefulSet recreates the same ordinal name and reattaches the same claim, while the Pod gets a new UID.
k8s-022.pitfall: Scaling the StatefulSet down and up to replace the Pod changes more than one Pod and is not the minimal operation.
k8s-022.verify: Only the Pod UID changed; name and claim binding are the same.

k8s-022.approach: Run only the read-only reader and hash the marker it reads.
k8s-022.why: If the claim was reattached, the bytes are unchanged and the hash equals h1.
k8s-022.pitfall: Running the writer again to check the file would recreate the evidence you are trying to verify.
k8s-022.verify: The reader hash equals the recorded initialization hash, with live values kept separate.

k8s-022.approach: For each deletion, name the deleted object and the policy that decides what happens next.
k8s-022.why: StatefulSet claim retention governs the PVC when the StatefulSet or replicas are removed, and the PV reclaim policy governs the volume when the claim is deleted.
k8s-022.pitfall: Calling Retain a backup ignores that the data still lives on one volume with no independent copy.
k8s-022.verify: Each deletion cites claim retention or PV reclaim, and retention is distinguished from backup.

k8s-022.approach: Read PVC events and binding status, then check the StorageClass provisioner, capacity and topology.
k8s-022.why: A Pending claim means no volume was bound, and the event usually names the missing class, capacity or zone.
k8s-022.pitfall: Deleting and recreating the claim discards the evidence and returns to the same Pending state.
k8s-022.verify: The check uses class, events or binding status and leaves the claim in place.

k8s-023.approach: Mark each object's scope and manager, from GatewayClass down to Pods.
k8s-023.why: GatewayClass is cluster scoped and tied to a controller, the Gateway is the platform listener and the HTTPRoute, Service and Pods belong to the application.
k8s-023.pitfall: Drawing the HTTPRoute as owning the Gateway reverses the parentRefs direction, where the route attaches to the listener.
k8s-023.verify: Each object shows scope and manager: controller, platform owner or application team.

k8s-023.approach: Read hostnames, matches path, parentRefs and backendRefs directly from the HTTPRoute.
k8s-023.why: These fields fully declare the route: lesson.example.test with prefix /version on lesson-gateway forwards to Service hello port 8080.
k8s-023.pitfall: Taking the backend port from the container port instead of backendRefs would cite 8080 by coincidence rather than from the route.
k8s-023.verify: Four values are quoted from their fields.

k8s-023.approach: Compare each parent's Accepted and ResolvedRefs observedGeneration with the route's generation.
k8s-023.why: Conditions are reported per parent, and only those at the current generation describe the current spec.
k8s-023.pitfall: Reading a True condition from an older generation would accept a route the controller has not yet seen.
k8s-023.verify: Each condition's observedGeneration equals metadata.generation for its named parent.

k8s-023.approach: Send /version and an unmatched path with Host lesson.example.test and record status and body.
k8s-023.why: Only requests matching hostname and prefix reach hello; others get the Gateway's no-route response.
k8s-023.pitfall: Omitting the Host header would fail both requests on hostname, hiding whether the path match works.
k8s-023.verify: /version returns the expected version, and the unmatched path never reaches hello.

k8s-023.approach: Verify with the supplied CA and expected hostname, then repeat with a mismatched identity.
k8s-023.why: Certificate verification checks both chain and name, so the wrong identity must fail at the TLS layer.
k8s-023.pitfall: Passing an insecure flag makes the mismatch succeed and proves nothing about the certificate.
k8s-023.verify: The valid case succeeds, and the wrong identity fails verification without bypass.

k8s-023.approach: List what the Ingress fixture needs, an ingressClassName and its controller, and the exact route UIDs to clean up.
k8s-023.why: Ingress and Gateway are separate APIs served by separate controllers, so one being ready says nothing about the other.
k8s-023.pitfall: Converting the HTTPRoute fields into an Ingress and assuming the same behavior ignores differences such as path match types.
k8s-023.verify: The list names class and controller, and cleanup cites exact UIDs.

k8s-024.approach: Open the base and both overlay kustomization.yaml files and point to resources and replicas.
k8s-024.why: The base supplies one Deployment, and each overlay's replicas entry sets 1 for dev and 2 for test.
k8s-024.pitfall: Editing replicas in the base would change both environments and erase the difference the overlays express.
k8s-024.verify: Each claim cites a resources or replicas entry in a named file.

k8s-024.approach: Run the pinned renderer, record its version and compare output with the expected JSON structurally.
k8s-024.why: Structural comparison ignores key order and formatting, so only real field differences remain.
k8s-024.pitfall: Comparing text by eye can miss a changed value or report reordered keys as a change.
k8s-024.verify: The version is recorded, and the structural comparison is clean or the tool is marked unavailable.

k8s-024.approach: Diff the dev and test renders and list every differing path.
k8s-024.why: The overlays only change replicas, so any other differing path reveals an unintended transform.
k8s-024.pitfall: Checking only that replicas differs would miss an extra label or image change.
k8s-024.verify: spec.replicas is the only differing path.

k8s-024.approach: Read managedFields for the contested field and name both managers with UID and resourceVersion.
k8s-024.why: Server-side apply records an owner per field, so a conflict shows two managers with competing intent for one path.
k8s-024.pitfall: Forcing conflicts takes ownership silently and the other manager may revert the field later.
k8s-024.verify: Both managers are named, and the conflict is reported rather than forced.

k8s-024.approach: Check the rendered namespace and image against the course allowlist before any apply.
k8s-024.why: A local render only proves the YAML is well formed; the course review decides whether the output may be applied.
k8s-024.pitfall: Treating a successful render as approval would apply a resource into another namespace or with an unapproved image.
k8s-024.verify: The escaping render is refused before apply.

k8s-024.approach: Record overlay source, renderer version, rendered hash, diff and any apply readback as separate items.
k8s-024.why: With source and tool version, a reviewer can regenerate the same hash and tell render evidence from cluster evidence.
k8s-024.pitfall: Saving only the apply output loses the link back to which overlay and renderer produced it.
k8s-024.verify: A reviewer reproduces the rendered hash from the recorded overlay and version.

k8s-025.approach: List Chart.yaml, values.yaml, values.schema.json, the single template and the expected output, and compare with a directory listing.
k8s-025.why: A chart with no dependencies, hooks or CRDs renders only what its one template declares.
k8s-025.pitfall: Inventorying from Chart.yaml alone misses a crds directory or a hook template that could install extra resources.
k8s-025.verify: The listing matches: no charts or crds directory and exactly one template.

k8s-025.approach: Record helm version and diff helm template output against expected-default.json structurally.
k8s-025.why: helm template renders locally without contacting a cluster, so the output reflects only chart and default values.
k8s-025.pitfall: Using helm install to see the output sends resources to a cluster before review.
k8s-025.verify: One Deployment with replicas 1 and the approved image, or the tool marked unavailable.

k8s-025.approach: Render with replicas 2 and diff the full object against the default.
k8s-025.why: The template only reads replicas from values, so the override should change exactly one path.
k8s-025.pitfall: Checking replicas alone would not detect a template that also changes labels with the value.
k8s-025.verify: spec.replicas is the only changed path.

k8s-025.approach: Render each invalid scratch values file and record the schema rule that rejects it.
k8s-025.why: Helm validates values against values.schema.json before rendering, so out-of-range, unapproved or unknown values fail locally.
k8s-025.pitfall: Removing the schema to make the render succeed disables the check the exercise relies on.
k8s-025.verify: Each file fails with a named schema rule, before any cluster operation.

k8s-025.approach: Search the render for helm.sh/hook annotations and any kind other than Deployment.
k8s-025.why: Hooks run outside normal install ordering, and cluster-scoped kinds exceed the worker's namespaced permissions.
k8s-025.pitfall: Installing and checking afterward lets a hook run before anyone reviewed it.
k8s-025.verify: Any hook or extra kind is flagged and the render is not installed.

k8s-025.approach: Record chart hash, values hash, renderer version and full diff, and keep apply evidence separate.
k8s-025.why: Hashes and the version pin every input, so a reviewer can reproduce the render offline.
k8s-025.pitfall: Recording only the release name ties the review to cluster state rather than reproducible inputs.
k8s-025.verify: A reviewer reproduces the render from the hashes and version without a cluster.

k8s-026.approach: Contrast replicas 2 on the Deployment with the DaemonSet's one Pod per eligible node.
k8s-026.why: A Deployment's count is fixed by spec.replicas, while a DaemonSet's desired count follows how many nodes pass its placement rules.
k8s-026.pitfall: Expecting the DaemonSet to honor a replicas field misreads its spec, which has none.
k8s-026.verify: On three nodes with two eligible, the Deployment yields 2 Pods and the DaemonSet yields 2, for different reasons.

k8s-026.approach: Check zone=a against each node's labels one at a time.
k8s-026.why: A nodeSelector requires an exact key and value match, so only nodes labeled zone=a pass.
k8s-026.pitfall: Treating a node with zone=b as close enough, or one missing the key as a wildcard, admits node-b wrongly.
k8s-026.verify: node-a yes, node-b no, node-c yes.

k8s-026.approach: For node-a and node-c, compare each node's taints with the Pod's tolerations.
k8s-026.why: A NoSchedule taint repels any Pod lacking a matching toleration, so node-c with the dedicated taint drops out.
k8s-026.pitfall: Assuming DaemonSets ignore all taints overgeneralizes; their automatic tolerations cover node condition taints, not a custom dedicated taint.
k8s-026.verify: Only node-a remains after both checks.

k8s-026.approach: Compare desiredNumberScheduled, numberReady and each Pod's nodeName with your predicted node list.
k8s-026.why: The DaemonSet controller computes desired placement itself, so its status and Pod nodeNames show whether reality matches your model.
k8s-026.pitfall: Checking only numberReady equals desiredNumberScheduled could pass even if the controller chose nodes you did not predict.
k8s-026.verify: Pod nodeNames match the predicted nodes, or a specific condition explains each difference.

k8s-026.approach: Replace the taint removal with a capability request or an unavailable placement report.
k8s-026.why: Node taints are shared cluster configuration, and removing one changes scheduling for every workload, not just this lab.
k8s-026.pitfall: Running kubectl taint with a trailing minus to make the Pod land edits a Node the learner does not own.
k8s-026.verify: The proposal modifies no Node and names the request or report used instead.

k8s-026.approach: Delete the DaemonSet by recorded UID and confirm its child Pods go with it.
k8s-026.why: Child Pods carry an ownerReference to the DaemonSet, so garbage collection removes them while node labels and taints stay as they were.
k8s-026.pitfall: Deleting Pods by label app could remove another agent's Pods, and the DaemonSet would just recreate its own.
k8s-026.verify: Owned UIDs are gone, and node labels and taints match the pre-run record.

k8s-027.approach: Write the SLI definition: which requests count, what counts as success, the window and the unit.
k8s-027.why: A definition precise enough to recount the five rows gives the same numerator and denominator to anyone who applies it.
k8s-027.pitfall: Saying the service was mostly fine gives no rule another person could apply to the ledger.
k8s-027.verify: Recounting the five rows yields the same two numbers.

k8s-027.approach: Count one 500 and four 200 among five eligible requests and divide each by five.
k8s-027.why: Under a rule that 5xx is an error, one of five is 0.2 errors and four of five is 0.8 success.
k8s-027.pitfall: Dividing by the four successful requests gives an error ratio of 0.25 and a denominator that excludes failures.
k8s-027.verify: The two fractions are 0.2 and 0.8, and they sum to one.

k8s-027.approach: Sort the five latencies and take rank ceil(q times n) for each quantile.
k8s-027.why: With n of 5, p50 uses rank 3 and p95 uses rank 5, so p95 is the largest of the five samples.
k8s-027.pitfall: Interpolating between ranks gives values that never appeared in the data and differ from the stated method.
k8s-027.verify: p50 is the third sorted value and p95 the fifth, matching 30 ms and 100 ms.

k8s-027.approach: Note that 3 is lower than 120 and check for a process restart between the readings.
k8s-027.why: Counters only increase within one process, so a drop after a restart is a reset, not negative traffic.
k8s-027.pitfall: Subtracting to report minus 117 requests treats a reset as real traffic.
k8s-027.verify: The record names the reset and uses only the evidence available for each interval.

k8s-027.approach: Record the metrics API error text next to the successful client result.
k8s-027.why: A missing metrics API means usage was not measured, which is different from a measured zero.
k8s-027.pitfall: Writing CPU 0 for the namespace converts an unavailable reading into a false measurement.
k8s-027.verify: The record contains the error or condition text and a separate passing client check.

k8s-027.approach: Pair one controller fact with one application metric, add a hypothesis and one reversible next check.
k8s-027.why: Together they connect what Kubernetes reported with what clients experienced, within a stated window and with object UIDs.
k8s-027.pitfall: Proposing a rollback as the next step makes the diagnosis irreversible before the hypothesis is tested.
k8s-027.verify: Units, window, UIDs and a reversible next check are all present.

k8s-028.approach: List storage class, CNI policy support, renderer, image and owned target with a host receipt or unavailable for each.
k8s-028.why: Each acceptance gate depends on one of these, so an unproven capability makes its gate untestable.
k8s-028.pitfall: Inferring NetworkPolicy support from the presence of a policy manifest tells you nothing about the CNI.
k8s-028.verify: Every row points to a receipt or reads unavailable.

k8s-028.approach: Capture the application response, marker hash and both client paths before the change, each with its source.
k8s-028.why: A baseline taken before the change lets every later gate compare like with like.
k8s-028.pitfall: Capturing baselines after the change cannot show whether the change altered them.
k8s-028.verify: Each baseline names a request, a hash or a client path and predates the change.

k8s-028.approach: Diff the full rendered output against the approved object list across kinds, namespaces, images, hooks and security fields.
k8s-028.why: The render is what will be applied, so a review of values alone could miss an added hook or a changed securityContext.
k8s-028.pitfall: Reviewing only the values diff assumes the templates turn values into exactly the expected fields.
k8s-028.verify: No unexpected kind, namespace, image, hook or security change appears.

k8s-028.approach: Write the boundary you expect to fail, apply the wrong probe path and compare with the first gate that fails.
k8s-028.why: A wrong readiness path keeps the new Pods unready, so the rollout gate should fail while data and policy stay unchanged.
k8s-028.pitfall: Applying the fault together with a policy change makes it impossible to tell which caused the failure.
k8s-028.verify: The first failing gate matches the prediction, and no unrelated object changed.

k8s-028.approach: Restore the reviewed probe, reread the marker with the reader and repeat both client paths.
k8s-028.why: Recovery must restore the application without touching the claim, so the hash stays h1 and policy outcomes repeat the baseline.
k8s-028.pitfall: Running the writer during recovery to be safe could change the marker and hide data loss.
k8s-028.verify: Hash equals h1, and the allowed and denied paths match the baseline.

k8s-028.approach: List removed UIDs and, separately, whether the PVC was retained and what reclaim applies.
k8s-028.why: Workload cleanup and data retention are separate decisions, and the claim may outlive the StatefulSet by policy.
k8s-028.pitfall: Saying everything was cleaned up hides whether the PVC and its bytes still exist.
k8s-028.verify: Removed UIDs and the PVC retention decision are recorded separately from cluster release.

k8s-029.approach: Read spec.scope in the CRD and metadata.namespace in the instance.
k8s-029.why: A CustomResourceDefinition is itself cluster scoped, while its scope field decides that LessonReport instances live in namespaces.
k8s-029.pitfall: Assuming the CRD is namespaced because its instances are confuses the registration with the objects it registers.
k8s-029.verify: CRD is cluster scoped, and hello-report has a namespace.

k8s-029.approach: Find each value in spec.group, spec.versions name, spec.names.kind, spec.names.plural and the instance metadata.name.
k8s-029.why: Group and version form the API path, kind is the type in YAML, plural is the URL segment and metadata.name names one object.
k8s-029.pitfall: Using the kind LessonReport in a URL instead of the plural lessonreports addresses a resource that does not exist.
k8s-029.verify: Five values come from five distinct fields.

k8s-029.approach: Check each candidate against required, type and range separately.
k8s-029.why: Structural schemas reject a string where an integer is required, a value outside the range and a missing required field.
k8s-029.pitfall: Expecting string 2 to be coerced to an integer assumes conversion the API server does not perform.
k8s-029.verify: Only integer 1 with an allowed message passes.

k8s-029.approach: Send the replcias typo with a named field validation mode and read the object back.
k8s-029.why: Depending on the mode, the server rejects the unknown field or prunes it, and in neither case is replicas set.
k8s-029.pitfall: Assuming the typo was stored as intent because the request succeeded ignores pruning.
k8s-029.verify: The readback is compared with the request, and the validation mode is recorded.

k8s-029.approach: Compare metadata.generation 7 with status.observedGeneration 6 before reading ready.
k8s-029.why: The status describes generation 6, so ready true says nothing yet about the spec at generation 7.
k8s-029.pitfall: Accepting ready true as current trusts a status that predates the latest change.
k8s-029.verify: Generation 7 is reported as not yet reconciled.

k8s-029.approach: Separate instance deletion by name and UID from CRD removal as a host operation.
k8s-029.why: Deleting the CRD deletes every instance of that type cluster wide, which exceeds learner scope.
k8s-029.pitfall: Running kubectl delete crd to clean up after one instance removes all LessonReports everywhere.
k8s-029.verify: Learner steps touch only the instance, and CRD removal is listed as a host step.

k8s-030.approach: Check whether the child exists, then compare its owner UID, then its configuration.
k8s-030.why: Ownership decides whether the controller may act at all, so a foreign child is refused before any comparison of fields.
k8s-030.pitfall: Comparing configuration first would update a foreign child that only happens to share a name.
k8s-030.verify: Absent creates, owned equal is no op, owned different updates and foreign refuses.

k8s-030.approach: Replay the same desired state three times and count create calls and children.
k8s-030.why: An idempotent reconcile creates once, and later passes find an owned equal child and do nothing.
k8s-030.pitfall: A reconcile that creates on every pass ends with three children for one desired object.
k8s-030.verify: One create, two no ops and one child.

k8s-030.approach: Change desired replicas from 1 to 2 and read observed state after each decision.
k8s-030.why: The first pass sees owned different and updates; the next sees owned equal and does nothing.
k8s-030.pitfall: Updating on every pass regardless of observed state never settles and floods the API.
k8s-030.verify: Update then no op, with the second decision following the first's effect.

k8s-030.approach: Compare the old child's owner reference UID with the new parent's UID.
k8s-030.why: Ownership is by UID, so a recreated parent with the same name does not own the old child.
k8s-030.pitfall: Matching on parent name would adopt a child that belongs to a deleted object.
k8s-030.verify: The UIDs differ, so the old child is foreign.

k8s-030.approach: Classify each case by whether retrying the same request unchanged could succeed.
k8s-030.why: Transient API errors can clear on retry with backoff, while invalid input fails the same way until intent changes.
k8s-030.pitfall: Retrying an invalid value with backoff loops forever without progress.
k8s-030.verify: Backoff applies to the transient case, corrected intent to invalid input, and stale status does not pass.

k8s-030.approach: Remove lesson.cleanup only after the external cleanup succeeds, leaving other.cleanup.
k8s-030.why: Each finalizer marks one owner's obligation, and the object is deleted only when the list is empty.
k8s-030.pitfall: Clearing the whole finalizer list skips other.cleanup's obligation and deletes the object early.
k8s-030.verify: After success only lesson.cleanup is gone; after failure the list is unchanged.

k8s-031.approach: Order authentication, authorization, admission and persistence, and stop at the first step that rejects.
k8s-031.why: Admission runs only for requests that were already authenticated and authorized, so an earlier refusal means the policy never evaluated.
k8s-031.pitfall: Citing a 403 Forbidden as proof the admission policy works confuses an RBAC denial with a policy denial.
k8s-031.verify: The sequence runs in that order and ends at the first rejecting step.

k8s-031.approach: Read matchConstraints and the binding namespace selector together and list each matched value.
k8s-031.why: The policy matches apps/v1 deployments on CREATE and UPDATE, and the binding narrows it to namespaces carrying the owned label.
k8s-031.pitfall: Expecting it to cover Pods created directly ignores that resourceRules name deployments only.
k8s-031.verify: The list shows apps, v1, deployments, CREATE, UPDATE and the labeled namespace.

k8s-031.approach: Evaluate the image check one container at a time and combine with all.
k8s-031.why: all returns true only when every element satisfies the predicate, so one unapproved image makes the whole expression false.
k8s-031.pitfall: Using exists instead of all would accept the mixed list because one approved image is enough.
k8s-031.verify: Approved only gives true and the mixed list gives false.

k8s-031.approach: Change only the image to an unapproved one, submit through the qualified path and read the Deployment back.
k8s-031.why: A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy denial stops the request before persistence, so the stored revision stays the same.
k8s-031.pitfall: Judging success by a missing new Pod could also come from a failed rollout of an accepted change.
k8s-031.verify: The message names the policy, and the readback shows the previous revision.

k8s-031.approach: Submit the approved source through the same path and record acceptance apart from any readiness result.
k8s-031.why: A positive control shows the policy admits valid input, so the earlier denial came from the image and not a broken path.
k8s-031.pitfall: Treating acceptance as application success skips the separate readiness and client checks.
k8s-031.verify: Acceptance is recorded, and readiness or client results appear as separate rows.

k8s-031.approach: Name fields the policy does not inspect, such as image digest signature and securityContext, and delete only host-owned UIDs.
k8s-031.why: The expression reads image strings only, so signatures and other workload kinds remain outside its scope.
k8s-031.pitfall: Claiming that all workloads are now verified extends the policy to resources and properties it never matched.
k8s-031.verify: Two uncovered fields are listed, and teardown names only the policy and binding UIDs.

k8s-032.approach: Apply app=hello to each of the three Pods' labels.
k8s-032.why: A PodDisruptionBudget counts only Pods its selector matches, so the unrelated Pod has no effect on the budget.
k8s-032.pitfall: Counting all three Pods in the namespace would overstate healthy Pods and allow an eviction the budget should block.
k8s-032.verify: Exactly the two hello Pods are selected.

k8s-032.approach: Subtract minAvailable 1 from healthy counts 2, 1 and 0 and floor at zero.
k8s-032.why: Allowed disruptions are the healthy Pods above the minimum, which can never be negative.
k8s-032.pitfall: Reporting minus 1 for zero healthy Pods suggests a debt the API does not track.

k8s-032.approach: Call the Eviction API with one selected healthy Pod and keep the response and the Pod's UID.
